newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Belarus ratify union, future still unclear.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Belarus ratify union, future still unclear.

text.p: The upper chambers of the Russian and Belarussian parliaments ratified a Union Treaty between the two Slavic ex-Soviet republics on Tuesday, taking another step towards closer integration.

Experts and politicians still argue about the final outcome of the loose union. Some say it is just a formality, others argue about its economic advantages and disadvantages for both states if agreements are fulfilled.
And Kremlin insiders say it could serve as a means for President Boris Yeltsin to win a third presidential term.

Under the Russian constitution Yeltsin cannot stand for a new term in 2000, but, if Russia and Belarus form a single state, he will have the right to contest the presidency of what would, technically, be a new country, they say.
No decision is likely soon, considering the shaky health record of the 66-year-old Russian leader who had a quintuple heart bypass operation last November.

In Moscow on Tuesday, 144 deputies in the Federation Council voted for the treaty and an accompanying charter, which formalise the loose union signed by Yeltsin and Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko last month. None voted against.
In Minsk, all 59 members of the Council of the Republic present at the session backed the deal.

"Belarussians and Russians have lived as one family for centuries," Alexander Dubko, governor of the Grodno region in western Belarus, told the chamber. "We are striking this union out of love, from the heart."
The lower houses in both states ratified the deal earlier.
The Belarussian parliament was set up by hardline Lukashenko after his victory in a controversial referendum last November which he used to expand his powers and rewrite the constitution.

The final union treaty was a watered-down version of an original draft, amended last month after liberals in the Russian government warned that the original could give hardliner Lukashenko too much power and damage Russia's interests.
Belarussian opposition nationalists refuse to recognise the new parliament in Minsk and are fiercely opposed to the deal, which they say is a sell-out of Belarussian interests.
In Russia many sceptics say that the economy of 10-million strong Belarus, where post-Soviet market reforms have barely started, will be a burden for the 150 million Russian citizens.
But most Russians and Belarussians, nostalgic for the Soviet Union, support integration moves between their two states.
In Russia, integration with Belarus is one of rare issues of accord between Yeltsin and the communist opposition.
Interfax news agency said Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov would visit Minsk on Wednesday to exchange ratification documents with Lukashenko.

Lukashenko, in an interview with Tuesday's Russian government newspaper Rossiiskaya Gazeta, said closer integration based on the accord would allow the Belarussian economy to grow by 40 percent and Russia's by 25 percent. He gave no time frame.
The two states would this year move to introduce unified tariffs on energy, communications and transport, he said. Tax systems would also be coordinated.
"A new inter-state regional grouping is being formed capable of protecting home industries in the domestic market and help them in the international one," Lukashenko said.
Yet on a very different note, speaking in parliament after the ratification, Lukashenko lashed out at Moscow, accusing unnamed ministers of "torpedoing" implementation of the treaty.
Chief among those seen as responsible for watering down the union is First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, whom Yeltsin appointed in March to push through new economic reforms.

Lukashenko told reporters after the session that if the situation did not improve, he would take it up later this week with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin -- whom he will meet at the Russian Black Sea resort of Sochi, where both will be taking a holiday.
